utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar. This is Thursday, August 20th, 2009, and I welcome Mr. Praljak, Mr. Prlic, Mr. Petkovic, and Mr. Stojic. Mr. Pusic is not with us for the moment for medical reasons. Of course I don't forget Mr. Coric, even though he is not with us. I welcome the counsels for Defence, all representatives of the OTP in this courtroom, as well as everyone helping us. Mr. Praljak, before giving the floor to Mr. Stringer, I have something to tell you to make sure that all hearings run smoothly in the future. I personally want to tell you once again that when a question is put to you, if you don't like the question, which might happen, well, think about it for a minute. If you believe that the question is not formulated correctly, which can happen, and I can tell you that sometimes when I put questions to you I always tell you don't hesitate to ask me to reformulate the question if you believe that I was wrong. However, if you believe that the question was not put correctly to you, don't get all het up immediately because the person putting the question to you might be insulted. Maybe when putting the question to you this person made a mistake without any hidden agenda behind it. This can happen to anyone. So please don't be suspicious immediately of bad intents. These are very complex matters, you know, and the person putting the question to you might very well have just made a mistake. If you find out that the question is not put correctly to you, don't -- it doesn't suit you, just answer very quietly. Just say, "I will answer your question, but for such and such reason I can't answer your question." But be very quiet, be very calm about it and everything will run smoothly. If you immediately become very harsh the person putting the question might feel insulted, and then we end up with what happened yesterday. I'm not a psychology professor, you know, but use a little psychology yourself when thinking about the person putting the question to you. I'm sure you understand all this. The people putting the questions to you are doing their job. They're in their own -- they're trying to understand what's happening. They might be in a wrong avenue and it's up to you to put them back on the right track if they were on the wrong track, but it might be a question that's embarrassing. You find -- you understand, you know that, and use your defence strategy to put the right answer to the question. I believe you understood, Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, the Honourable Chamber, I assure you - and I repeat - from the very beginning to the very end, no amount of psychology at all has been involved in the way that I've been answering questions, none at all. As soon as a question enters my head, my logic comes to grips with it, and I realise that by providing a certain kind of answer I might violate facts or indeed violate a good logic for answering such questions. I try to answer questions like that irrespective of the person asking the question, with no ill intention whatsoever. If that was the way I came across to Judge Trechsel or anyone else yesterday, my deepest apologies. That's all I've got to say. It's got nothing to do with psychology. It's just the way I think, the way I reason. Will I present my facts and will the logic of my answer be a valid one in terms of explaining the same facts to sufficient degree to be able to get at the truth and meet the needs of justice. I want no more and no less than that. Anything else that may or may not occur during this drawn up process that might be unpleasant or undesirable is certainly not through my own doing or because I so intend. Sometimes because this is an arduous process, there is a certain amount of spill-over and effects arise that are not desirable which might be confusing to the people listening to me, but I'm telling you why this is. That has been the story of my entire life, and this is the own reason for it. I perceive a question and the person asking the question no longer has anything to do with it. The question becomes a part of my body and my mind. All I have is the best effort I can make to answer the question. What exactly happened, what the circumstances were, unfortunately, given the nature of the war, the circumstances were far too many for me to define in a single sweep. There were social circumstances and factors at work too. Sometimes when I try too hard to understand someone, I'm afraid this might result in me telling something that is not strictly speaking true. That is the kind of misunderstanding that I'm trying to prevent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I take due note of all of this. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just one minute, Your Honours. In light of yesterday's exchange, just for clarification purposes because I do need to -- to consult extensively with Dr. Prlic concerning what I perceive in retrospect to be an invitation or potential invitation by the Trial Chamber or by the President, before I could give proper thought and advice to my client, I would need to know more specifically what the Trial Chamber's intent is, what the modalities are, and of course the Prosecution, as I understand it, would want to be heard. So that's something that perhaps the Trial Chamber should consider and then get back to us on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, yesterday when I wanted to talk to Mr. Prlic, I did convey correctly that I was the one putting the question personally, and I even used the conditional tense in French saying that I was personally putting the question. As of today the Trial Chamber doesn't have a position on this topic. It hasn't been dealt with yet, but as far as I'm concerned as a Judge, sometimes I make proposals to my colleagues, you know, in order to find solutions. I make suggestions. And before making these suggestions, first I have to be absolutely sure of a few elements. I have to collect these elements. And then in a possible suggestion that I could make to my colleagues, I needed to know whether the element that there might have been a theoretical possibility for Mr. Prlic if he came as a witness, as a court witness, he would testify on his own report, then if I had obtained his agreement on that, I would have been able to tell my colleagues, well, there is a possibility, a theoretical possibility that exists to integrate this report into our procedure. This is an element in Mr. Prlic's defence case, and the legal solution that we could find could be him coming as a court witness. I was at the very beginning of all this -- of all this thought process. So in French, I'm sure you understand some French now, and French is very precise and there are a lot of nuances in French possible, so in French I had used a conditional tense saying if, if, if, possibly, and then also I added that this was very personal, this was a personal suggestion. Of course the -- Mr. Stringer is American, and unfortunately he doesn't completely grasp all the nuances of French. He thought this was the real position of the Trial Chamber, but no absolutely not. This was not the position of the Trial Chamber expressed. It was myself who had in my own mind said that there might have been a procedural possibility to integrate the report later on. That's as far as it went. So yesterday you stood up immediately and there you felt aggressed, I don't know. Maybe you hadn't really understood what I had meant, but this was a very personal approach, this was a very personal suggestion in order to know -- have all the elements at hand in order to tell my colleagues later on, there might be this possibility and then we could discuss on about it, either we will agree on it or not. That was as far as it went. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karnavas, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but I simply would like to confirm that there is no change in the Chamber's position so far on this matter. This issue has not been discussed and as it was again outlined by President Judge Antonetti, we had not discussed this matter and there is no change in the position as taken before. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, and thank you, Mr. President. I certainly wish to convey my apologies for perhaps being overly quick. It's unusual for me to be in court where a Judge directly addresses my client and bypasses me. I must say it hasn't happened before, and so for the Trial Chamber to directly address my client caused me a bit of anxiety. Be that as it may, we remain flexible and open to all sorts of possibilities. Let me just say that. However, for me to properly advise my client, we would need to know what the position is of the Trial Chamber at some point. So I -- if the Trial Chamber were to come to some sort of a position at some point, then I would be in a position to properly advise. I need more information. I don't want to deal with hypotheticals, especially with someone, you know, Dr. Prlic's background. Being a diplomat, he doesn't deal in hypotheticals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I do not always agree with you, but this time I do and I understand fully well that this looked like a bait and you of course had to jump. That was absolutely understandable. I would suggest that we leave the matter now, and if the Chamber sees a possibility or envisages any change in its previous decisions in this matter, it would signal this to you, and you would then sort of see not green light but yellow. For the time being, I think it's still red.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Which doesn't mean that you can't consult with Mr. Prlic, of course. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning. Good morning, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone else around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I see that you don't have the binder that we were working with yesterday, and so I'm going to ask if the registrar could provide you with the binder that we had yesterday. It was binder 1 of 2. If it's binder number -- list number 5. That's right. Thank you. It's the larger one there. And, General, if you want to take a moment. We were looking at Exhibit P04131. And I believe from your testimony yesterday, General, you told us that you, I guess in coordination with General Petkovic, issued this order. I think you might have been in the field somewhere and he was the one who signed it for you or something like that but that you accepted this as an order of yours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I do accept it as my order. Back in prison, which I have by now begun to call home, I was trying to think back, and I realised at one point that I had not made [as interpreted] in time to sign this document. There was a war on. By the 13th, powerful attacks had been launched by the BH Army in the south Mostar area. For some reason of military urgency, I hadn't made it in time to sign this document but the order reflects that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And we were working our way through this yesterday, and I would like to continue. Yesterday we spoke about the operative zones being directly subordinated to the Main Staff as indicated in paragraph 2, and then yesterday also we talked about the Bruno Busic and the Ludvig Pavlovic regiments, if you'll recall, and you indicated I believe also that those two units were directly subordinated to the Main Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. This order requires that that be done, and it was supposed to be done. If you'd like me to, I can provide an explanation about the background of this order and why it was drawn up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, let me just take you through the various units that are identified, and that's primarily what I'm interested in. The next unit that's -- that's indicated here is the rocket and artillery regiment, and is it correct, General, that pursuant to this order the rocket and artillery regiment is one of the units that's directly subordinated to the HVO Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the artillery. This was meant to establish the full control, and that's why I asked that some of the artillery units be resubordinated and placed under the command of the Main Staff in order for us to achieve effective control to make sure they weren't doing anything outside my control. Some of the artillery had to remain in the operation zones and in the brigades themselves, but I wanted to some elements from the artillery to be under my control just in case a cease-fire was signed. So I made sure they weren't firing any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. General --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I wanted to make sure that no one would be firing when not allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you a questions -- a few questions to follow up on what you've just said. So you're talking about some of the artillery units be resubordinated and placed under the command of the Main Staff. So are we talking about individual or different units, artillery units, that were placed in different locations throughout the -- the zone of conflict? For example, perhaps some artillery units up in the North-west Herzegovina operative zone, other units down in south-east with Colonel Lasic? So these are different artillery units that were located in different places?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't really say different units. The artillery was, of course, a single whole throughout that area. Command and control over that unit is exercised by the zone commander. There are certain mortars that belong to a brigade, for example, or a battalion. When you say different artillery units, I am not sure I agree with the use of that term. There were several guns involved, long-range guns, and those were the only ones that I wanted placed under my control.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It seems to me that you're implying that prior to the date of this order, these artillery pieces were under the direct control of the operative zone commanders; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes. Look, Mr. Stringer, they remained under the zone commands. The commander of the Main Staff or one of his deputies, for example, are facing an incipient attack, and now they're waiting for this artillery to start being used. It's not what it was like. Nevertheless, I wanted to acquire a certain degree of control over these pieces and then they had to go to my deputy or me or the Chief of the Main Staff. Some things are happening, they should put it that way, and we need long-range artillery to respond. These would have been too few still, but nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: When we talk about artillery here, maybe we should specify what types of weaponry we are discussing. Are we talking about everything from -- from mortars up to howitzer? Can you describe for us the weaponry that you're referring to when you talk about artillery?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three or four 130-millimetre guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Then are you saying that the -- well, when -- just for the record when you say 130-millimetre guns, that is something different than mortar weaponry; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very much so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So 130-millimetre guns, your intention was to put those under more direct control of the Main Staff, whereas weaponry such as mortars was going to remain more directly under the control of the operative zone or the brigade that had those mortars?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, not just the mortars. All the other artillery as well, the 105-millimetre guns, the tanks, and so on and so forth. You can't take these things out of the operative zone because that would make it impossible to run the army in a properly structured way. Even what occurred was not really an established military practice. The commander of an operative zone is responsible for his area and the brigade commander is responsible for his own sector. One cannot afford to bide their time and wait every time they want to respond to a rocket launcher attack or a mortar attack or a 105-millimetre gun attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me if I intervene. I think we have again a little problem of translation, because in the English text we have rocket and artillery regiment, which gives the impression of a relative large unit just under the brigade, between brigade and battalion, under one command which has probably one or two units of rockets and several units of howitzers, 130-millimetre guns, you name it. Now, if I look at the original text I see RTP, which we also have in the translation, but then in quotation marks, something which I tried to read as "Zrakoplovna Grupa," and that seems to me to be much less technical an expression than rocket and artillery regiment. Would you agree, Mr. -- what is your reaction to this, Mr. Praljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there's a comma there. There is the regiment and there's the "Zrakoplovna Grupa," two different things. In my opinion one of the chief problems here is something that I've mentioned before. The rocket and artillery regiment, when you put it like that, that's accurate and can be translated into something that exists in other armies across the world, but what do you really have there? What did it mean in practical terms in the HVO, and what does that mean when you compare it to the norms and standards that prevail in the US army or the French army? It really had nothing to do with it. We just used these terms. So the meaning was transferred from these other armies, normal armies, to the HVO, and that's where misunderstandings occurred, considerable ones. There were two 130-millimetre guns that actually worked, that were operational, as far as I remember. What I wanted to achieve was to get them a little more under control, that was all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Was there a command for this group, "grupa"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. They were subordinated to the commander of the operation zone, then obviously he was the one in this area that had the power to say target this or target that, and he still could. But if there was any communication that he had with the Main Staff, obviously he would have needed to raise the question first. I didn't entirely make it impossible for him to use these. It would not have been logical or indeed possible. Nevertheless, whenever he had an opportunity to be in touch with me, Petkovic, or Tole, he would invariably say, There is an attack going on here or there. There is a concentration of units, there is enemy artillery activity from these locations are those. I seek approval to respond with three, four, or five shells. Even whenever he was not able to get in touch directly, he would have still been allowed and entitled to use these pieces anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Did you use the word "mortar shell" now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's what I thought in the context, so again the translation is perhaps not fully precise. Thank you. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, in the -- in the English that we just got, you were talking about when a commander would come to you for permission, and we were given the word "a mortar shell," and that's the reason why Judge Trechsel followed up, because we're not talking about mortar here. We're talking about a commander who wants to fire a shell from a 130-millimetre cannon or gun. That's the only weaponry we're talking about here when we talk about your intention to place certain artillery under the direct commander of the Main Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Nevertheless, and I do have to repeat this, if it was possible to reach me, Petkovic, or Tole without necessarily precluding the possibility, if for whatever reason it wasn't possible, because of the powerful attacks and the poor state of our communications, the commander of the operation zone would have been entitled to use these. I will explain later on what actually happened. Mortars are anti-infantry weapons, and you can't take them out of a unit when someone's attacking and then you respond by firing mortars. That's supposed to prevent infantry from advancing. It's impossible to separate them from the command of a unit in which the actual weapons are multiple rocket launchers, mortars. These are infantry weapons. They have to be used swiftly, and there is no time to make phone calls, try to speak to someone, and such like.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So then to just to try to sum this up, can we agree that your intention here in this order in respect of the artillery is for the Main Staff to exert greater control over the use of 130-millimetre guns, recognising that under certain circumstances it may be appropriate for an operative zone commander to use one of these gun us without first seeking permission from the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. If unable to get in touch with anyone from the Main Staff, they might just use it, under the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And that smaller guns, such as 105-millimetre guns, mortars, multiple-rocket launchers, those weapons at all times remained under the direct control of the operative zone.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the operative zone and the brigade command, too. 60-millimetre, 82-millimetre mortars, under the command of the battalion, whoever they were attached to. These are anti-infantry weapons for the most part. They had to be used immediately with immediate effect. They're always within a unit, and this unit that has these weapons exercises command over those pieces as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And so that because the operative zones, the brigades, the battalions fall under the chain of command of the Main Staff, then those smaller weapons that you've just described now would remain indirectly within the chain of command of the Main Staff. Right? They're just one or two steps further down the chain from the Main Staff, whereas the 130-millimetre guns, the intention was to place those guns at the level the Main Staff in most circumstances; is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, well, Mr. Stringer, I give you an accurate explanation and then you talk about most situations. I'm talking about a very specific situation. If they're not able to get in touch to establish communication, they have the right to use anything that's available to them to defend. Nevertheless, there was some cease-fires there. We didn't look at my document when there were several artillery pieces that I placed under my command in terms of them being under an obligation to report to me whenever wanting to fire a shell or two, when the enemy forces were concentrated. That was during some of the cease-fires that were happening. I wanted to establish full control to keep someone, something from firing a bullet or a shell, and then the other side would say violation of the cease-fire and so on and so forth. I think I'm perfectly clear about this, and I've told you everything about the exact circumstances under which --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sorry to cut you off, I -- perhaps you misunderstood my question or I didn't ask it well enough, because I think we have established and were clear actually on what was the intention and the situation in respect of the 130-millimetre guns. I was -- my follow-up question or the last question was more directed at the -- the other forms of weaponry, the 105, the 60s, and the mortars and the RPGs which remained within the brigade or the battalion, and as to those weapons, simply the question was that those were indirectly under the chain of the -- or they were -- remained within the chain of command of the Main Staff, but they were just farther down the chain. Isn't that a correct way of putting it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in part. Look, everything is within the chain of command of the Main Staff. RPG is a weapon which a soldier is issued with. A soldier would have been in charge with these pieces. When under attack, obviously, formally speaking, it's all within the chain of command of the Main Staff. Nevertheless, I'm not sure how to simplify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No. I think you've answered my question there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I'm still trying to imagine how this was going to work and my tentative hypothesis is that this order is a bit helter-skelter order. It's not really a well-established military order. For instance, the artillery pieces are not individual guns with few people to operate it, but there is some infrastructure with it, there are normally vehicles that can put it into position. One speaks of wheels and barrels in control of artillery, and the ammunition is quite an issue because its heavy and so forth. There is also normally infantry protection of the positions and so forth. Does this perhaps mean what you say here, that you take control of the barrels, that is to say you say the General Staff principally can stop shooting and order shooting secondary to, in certain cases, also the operation zone, but the administration, the infrastructural part remains with the OZ. Is that a correct interpretation of what you had in mind when you signed this order, when you formulated this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's just right, Your Honour. It remains in the OZ. It then requests ammunition from the logistics base, whatever they could provide. 95 per cent of the time the guns remained, they are rooted to the spot without being moved anywhere. If I may just add this: This order was primarily written because the system of command in the operation zones was beginning to cave in. If you remember the document that I produced about the 21 units near Gornji Vakuf, and then you asked how come you were exercising command over a battalion or a company over there. That was precisely what was beginning to fall apart. This order within the whole thing, the operation zone, the brigade, and so on and so forth. I was angry, I do remember, so I went to see Petkovic. You see, at one point in time when this system was crumbling, you had to do two things: First you react in order to save the day along the front line, but what you keep trying to do throughout all the time is bring order back to a system that should be there. At one moment you command a company because there is nothing else you can do to defend a certain area, but at the same time you're trying to bring order back to the system, alter the part of the system that you will not be commanding but rather the battalion commander, a brigade commander, an operation zone commander, because of the fact that these units were scattered over the area because people were exhausted, men were exhausted, because of insubordination. Because of a system that was on the verge of a total breakdown, I had to do two things at the same time. The needs of the moment, on the one hand, and re-establishing the entire system and getting it up and running again so to speak. So this is an attempt to say the zone commanders are these and this here is what we will be forwarding to the Main Staff. I'm not sure if that makes it any clearer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. You have long ago answered satisfactory my question. Thank you. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I have just one brief follow-up question, which is a technical one. If I have understood correctly, the artillery, 130-millimetre artillery, you say that this was placed under the responsibility of the Defence Department, and from what I understood, there were three such guns. Was it three guns? You had three artillery pieces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I remember, that was bidden [as interpreted] in reference to the operation zone around Mostar, first and foremost East Herzegovina. I think there were three. That's the way I remember it. But then you said under the Defence Department. It's not the Defence Department. It's the Main Staff. I think you misspoke there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Main Staff. So this is not the Defence Department. Right. Now, these three artillery pieces, you mean there are three broad categories. You have the Soviet M-46 artillery pieces or the American artillery pieces, howitzers 155-millimetres. Were these American or Russian artillery pieces that you had? You don't know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some were Russian, some American. There were some guns there that came from America back in 1954 when Stalin and Tito clashed. The Americans provided Yugoslavia with over 8.000 barrels or guns that were still being used, and we had some of those. All sorts of different calibres needless to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, let's continue on. I think yesterday we -- I'm not going to spend any real time on the air force group. I believe you indicated yesterday that that was essentially helicopters that were used to transport wounded people and that those, your intention was to make sure that those were under the direct control of the Main Staff. Is that a correct statement on the air force reference here?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those helicopters were used for transport alone to transport wounded people during my time as commander. I never allowed myself to use the helicopter to get from one place to another. It was just for the wounded, those from Mostar, those from Central Bosnia, those from Rumboci right next to Rama, and so on and so forth. Many men killed, many men wounded. It was quite a problem to get them all safely to somewhere else and to save their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, the next reference here, and I'll read from my translation, and hopefully it will correspond to the original language version, and again just to repeat, this is part of paragraph 2 of your order in which you're ordering that the Main Staff exerts direct command over certain units, and here we get down to the Tuta ATG, and then I have: "... artillery and DTG, sabotage-terrorist groups, outside operative zones and brigades." General, what you're saying there, are you saying that the Main Staff has direct control or command over the Tuta ATG until that group or part of it is actually deployed to a combat position within an operative zone or brigade, and then at that point it becomes under the direct control of the people on the ground there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Tuta ATG is actually Baja Kraljevic, you know, Predrag Mandic. To be quite frank, I don't know why this reads Tuta ATG. It's used colloquially, probably, but it was Baja Kraljevic. I'm sorry? Baja Kraljevic, yes. Predrag Mandic, of course, I knew him from 1992, an outstanding fighter, an invalid of war. He lost an eye. As for this, the ATG outside the operation zones, quite frankly when the operative system of the units in Jajce, for example, and cities that were lost, near Travnik and so on, began to crumble, at one point in time people belonged to no one at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, General --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You're giving -- you're giving more detail than I really need at this point. Are you saying that for purposes of this order the Tuta ATG is the same thing as the Baja Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. This group referred to as Tuta is actually the Baja Kraljevic unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but given the fact that you're on your own today, Mr. Stringer, I would like to draw your attention to the translation. There appears to be an error, a serious one, and I think you have just been dwelling on that portion. I'm talking about the translation of the document. Item 2 of the order under discussion, the portion that you are now discussing, it reads: "RTP, the air force group, and then the Tuta ATG," and then they go on to talk about ATG -- DTG, and so on and so forth, and in English it's ATG Tuta/artillery. Some artillery is there in the English document, which makes it appear as though the Tuta ATG was about artillery, but that is nowhere to be found in the original. You can check the abbreviations in the Croatian original. Tuta ATG, no artillery there. The next thing that follows is DTG. I'm just saying this because it may give rise to a certain amount of confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I suggest that we ask the general simply to read the remainder of the paragraph in his own language starting with the words: "The air force group..."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, could you just read starting with "The air force group," just read the rest of the paragraph for us. Read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The air force group," in inverted commas, "The air force group, and the Tuta ATG, and the DTG, outside the composition of the operation zones and brigades."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So my question then about the Tuta --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I'm sorry. There is just one thing that I'd like to clarify. We have a problem on the transcript now. The air force group, line 12, the air force group, the air force group, and the Tuta ATG. This "many" does not exist. There is the air force group, ATG, Tuta, Tuta again in inverted commas. The general should re-read this portion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Inverted commas "The air force group," and RTG -- ATG Tuta, under quotation marks, and DTG outside the composition of the operation zones and brigades. Not DFG -- all right. It's been amended. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There seems to be another error because RTG has been added on before ATG.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me just -- I'll try as best I can to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, starting with the air force, your intention here is to place the air force, the Tuta ATG, and the DTG, those three groups, there are three different units or groups, the air force, the Tuta ATG, and thirdly the DTG, those are the three groups that are referred to in this part of your order; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And those are three different units or groups.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then as to two of those, as to the Tuta ATG and the DTG, those are under the direct command of the Main Staff when they are found outside one of the operative zones or brigades; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. If I may, these are men who were away from the front for a while with no weapons on them, living as civilians. But if they were not available in some facility or other, for example, the Ludvig Pavlovic facility in Capljina, or something like that, and then -- for example, there was the problem of the breakthrough by the BH Army south of Mostar, and when the commander of the operation zone, Mico Lasic, could not issue an order to Ludvig Pavlovic, rather, they ask that Ludvig Pavlovic be resubordinated to him for that particular assignment. And someone from the Main Staff would draft an order, Ludwig Pavlovic hereby resubordinated to the commander of the operations zone, Lasic, to carry out a task in Blagaj, south of Mostar, or wherever else. The units were not more mobile.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then is it correct, General, that the intention was to establish or affirm the same procedure in terms of the Tuta ATG and the DTG?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Baja Kraljevic, it was supposed to be the same procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So after the Main Staff ordered or agreed that, say, this unit the Tuta ATG or the Baja Kraljevic, after the Main Staff agreed or ordered that it would be deployed to certain operative zone or brigade, once that unit arrived at the operative zone or brigade, they would then fall under the direct command of that operative zone or brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Normally the sector, each theatre of war has it's own sector. If they were sent to a sector, then the sector commander would assume command over those.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We talked about the military police a little bit we'll talk about the military police more later but is it correct that this system in place, for example, the Tuta ATG, Baja Kraljevic ATV [sic], it's a little bit similar or it is indeed quite similar to an analogous situation that existed as to military police units that could be deployed in an operative zone on the approval of the Defence Department, but once that military police unit arrived at the operative zone, it would be for operative purposes subordinated to the operative zone or the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. It was subordinated in an operative sense. They had a task. They went about carrying out this task as soon as the as task was completed, and during the execution of the task itself when they weren't -- well, they were what they were, military policemen. Therefore, this is a dual role, as simple as that. They weren't all deployed along the front line. They worked in shifts. They were taking turns. One battalion was providing manpower. You can't just be in a trench for 24 hours at a time. It's very difficult to cope with an experience like that, and it's not quite well, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, let me give you another example. You said that you knew nothing about Doljani and Sovici. So this is a purely theoretical question. If the ATG Tuta was in Sovici and Doljani, this means that he must have been resubordinated to the commander of the operational zone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the Tuta ATG was there. Therefore, I can't say either way. Baja Kraljevic, that's the one I'm talking about. I'm not sure what exactly could be behind this name. To me this was the Baja Kraljevic unit, as I said. But when you send the unit to a certain area, it is accurate to say that they are resubordinated to the sector commander. If this is an area covered by a brigade or by zone, of course there are different degrees involved. I cannot simplify this any further. There is a sector commander. This is the smallest unit -- in a battalion, is the smallest unit that could be entrusted with a sector. If someone comes there, for example, if the brigade commander happens to be within the sector too, then he's the one exercising the command. If there are large-scale clashes going on in the operational zone, commander would come over and say I'm commanding these or I'm commanding those and then often so on and so forth. And this is the sort of thing that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. General, I've finished with that document, but I do want to just stay with the same issue for a couple more minutes. I want to take you back to some of your testimony earlier in this trial which you gave on the 23rd of June of this year. I'm on page 41865 of the transcript, and here you're talking about the artillery or the mortar weapons in Mostar town. Let me just read to you what you said on the 23rd of June. You said: "I claim that on my order and on the order of my commanders there was a minimal number of responses to their shelling, and when we did that it was selective. We never targeted or hit the hospital, because I never allowed my artillerymen to target their mortars, which were placed there strategically and intentionally, hoping that we would miss and that we would target and hit the hospital, and then the whole world would talk about the criminal HVO." General, when you said that you had communications and you gave orders in respect of the use of artillery and mortars in Mostar, are you telling us that you in fact did, as the commander of the HVO Main Staff, have command authority over the artillery and the mortars that were positioned in Mostar town after the 24th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, unfortunately it's entirely impossible to answer this question. It's impracticable. I said what I said and I stand by that. Based on what I was endlessly repeating and requesting, hoping that they would hear me out, that they shouldn't, that they couldn't. You can't issue orders of that kind, because fundamentally this is inherent to the rules of war that I adhered to. But whenever I saw my commanders and my soldiers, and I spent all of my time among my soldiers and my commanders, each day, each minute, each break they took, I kept telling them how to fight, what the rules were that applied, and about all the ways in which we should not be fighting and must not be fighting. It was based on all of that, and because I felt their understanding and in a way even respect. There were only ever perhaps exceptional and very sporadic violations, if at all. And the reason for that is simple, Mr. Stringer, I was convinced --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, the Judges will make their findings about the number of incidents or whether there were crimes involved in the shelling of Mostar. I'm more interested in your relationship to the people who were using the artillery and the mortars in Mostar. Now, what you're telling us, sir, isn't it true, is that you had direct communications, direct contacts with, and you knew who -- and were in charge of the people who were using the HVO artillery and mortars in the Mostar town; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That cannot be true during a war, in any case, not the way you put it. There is and chain of command. There is a system of use of pieces. It is known who issues orders, at what level, and with what purpose. What I am talking about was an example I gave you, and I was trying to educate those using it how to use it. People learn about how they should behave in the course of a war. As for the use itself, the way you put it, that I was at each and every mortar position and knew every operator, that is a question that I cannot answer in any meaningful way. What were they to do if they were in Mostar and came under attack and I was elsewhere in a different location? It is impossible to answer that, not in the situation of such a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But what you told us on the 23rd of June, and I'm quoting, you said: "I never allowed my artillerymen to target their mortars." And you say target their mortars. I believe you're saying you never allowed your artillerymen to target the mortars on the ABiH side. But what that means, General, is that you in fact did exert directly command and control over the HVO artillery that were positioned in Mostar town. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is completely incorrect. Direct command over each artillery piece is exercised by the commander who was initially assigned by that piece. I was trying to educate them by conversing with them. You can say there are mortars at -- next to the hospital. Fire at them irrespective of how many shells would land on that hospital. In any case, that would be permissible under the laws of war, because the guilty side is the one keeping mortars next to the hospital. The guilty side is the one placing its command posts among the people. Command posts are military targets which may be destroyed. But still I told my men, Do not target those positions, because that would amount to civilian casualties. Only if you come under a direct threat, respond with a minimum number of shells. I was simply trying to educate them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So you were educating them as the commander of the HVO Main Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was trying to teach them how to wage a war even in situations in which the enemy side is using civilians as a shield. We can see what the regular armies of other countries behave in the wars nowadays.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General. General, sorry, but you're starting to move away, too far away.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Because they were HVO artillery and mortars, they fell within the chain of command of the HVO Main Staff which you were commanding; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is incorrect, incorrect and absurd in the military sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me repeat the question, because I respectfully don't agree at all with what you've just claimed, and in fact, it's completely inconsistent with what you've already told us. You've already told us a few minutes ago that the HVO artillery, and the mortars, the guns, big and small, were all within the chain of command of the Main Staff; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chain of command of the Main Staff. Well, everything was within that chain, but that doesn't answer the question who issues orders about the use.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I understand that, General, and I think that we're -- we're talking at cross-purposes. I'm not claiming that you were boots on the ground in West Mostar 24/7 telling people where to shoot their artillery guns and mortars, but the fact is that you were the highest-ranking HVO commander responsible for the HVO artillery and mortar that were deployed and used in Mostar. Isn't that true, from the 24th of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what sense responsible? What does that word mean militarily speaking? I do not understand your question, not in the least. It misses its target completely in the military sense. It goes against the structure of any army, including the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In the military chain of command of the HVO, the HVO artillery and mortars that were deployed in Mostar town fell within the direct chain of command of the HVO Main Staff. True or not true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you a hundred times that that is incorrect. Each piece is assigned to a person who has his first superior, second superior, third superior, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, if you look at your last question, perhaps you want to reformulate, because here you put together artillery and mortars and direct commander, whereas earlier on you have made, and I think correctly so, a distinction, artillery, direct mortars, indirect. So I think it is dangerous to -- to mix it up like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'll reformulate. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm talking about the chain of command, General, the chain of command. All right? Just work with me here, if I can borrow one else's phrase. No, no, let me ask --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me ask --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mortars are artillery pieces as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. General, let me ask a series of questions, and I'll do my best to be as clear and as specific as I can. The HVO had artillery. For purposes of this conversation the artillery consists of 160-millimetre guns, 105-millimetre guns, some 60-millimetre guns, mortars, and multiple-rocket launchers, and maybe there are other pieces as well.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no 160-millimetre guns, and there are no 60-millimetre guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. You tell me what was the HVO artillery. Tell me everything you had.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. There are documents to that effect. I'm supposed to enumerate everything 18 years later? There were 60-millimetre mortars, 82-millimetre mortars, 120-millimetre mortars. There were some tanks which were mostly used as artillery. There was some 105-millimetre guns, some 76-millimetre guns. There were multiple-rocket launchers of 105-millimetres. As far as I know in the zone around Mostar there were 3 130-millimetre guns. There were several guns of 155 or 152-millimetre calibre. More or less, that was the HVO artillery. At some point, I asked together with Petkovic to control these 130-millimetre guns in the area of Mostar town. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I simply asked you what were the -- what was the artillery. You told us. Now, my next question is this: The other day we were looking at the chart of the HVO structure, and there was a box for the Defence Department and there's another box for the Main Staff. Is it correct that all of the HVO artillery that you've just identified, we can put that in the box of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, in Mostar town, from the time you became commander of the HVO Main Staff, to the best your recollection what HVO artillery was in Mostar town?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Mostar town itself there were no artillery pieces. One doesn't keep artillery pieces in a town but outside because of their greater range, and we did not place artillery pieces in proximity to civilians as opposed to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Then tell me what were the locations of HVO artillery in West Mostar, on the west side of the Neretva River in the area of the town of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: To repeat, in Mostar town we did not have artillery pieces. As for questions such as this, Mr. Stringer, one needs a map and documents, and you can ask me to prepare all that for you, although I don't know why I should do that. The weapons were placed in certain locations outside Mostar town. Now, I would have to be able to recall all that and go through all the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, what are the locations that you've just referred to where the HVO artillery was deployed, recognising that you could move it around.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seven or eight kilometres or ten kilometres as the crow flies from the Neretva. You -- we have to check that on the map and see where the individual positions were. It is always best that mortars be behind a hill, because then they are not directly visible and their trajectory is such that it -- the shell goes up and then lands, but it's up to artillerymen to choose their positions according to the best angle they can cover, the best protection they can get to protect themselves against enemy artillery. They try not to be detected by way of hiding the fumes or the flames which occur when shells are fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection what are the HVO artillery pieces? What types of artillery were directed at Mostar town?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing was directed at Mostar town. It was directed at the positions of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. One moves barrels to the point where the attack on their part began so as to repel that attack and to cause --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, you didn't -- you didn't --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- losses --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- which would deter them from --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- you're becoming really evasive now, you're not answering my questions. I asked you a specific question. What types of artillery pieces -- I'll rephrase it, if it will make happy, what specific HVO artillery pieces were deployed for targeting ABiH positions in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were 60-millimetre mortars, 82-millimetre mortars, 120-millimetre mortars. There were some RPG weapons of 105 calibre or perhaps 125 calibre. There were 76-millimetre guns called ZIS, these are smaller calibre guns. There were tanks, a few of them, and they moved from one position to the next according to the need, and they were mostly used as artillery pieces unless they were malfunctioning because these were old tanks of Russian make, T-55s dating back to World War II. That was it pretty much, and there were of course the 130-millimetre guns. There were two or three of them. I think at first we had two and perhaps another one arrived later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Was there a T-55 tank positioned at a place called Stotina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea. I did not position tanks over -- across the operational zone. A tank can come and go a dozen times a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And you should put that question to someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So from what you've said that -- from what you've said, there were no 130-millimetre guns directed at HVO positions in East Mostar. So then does that mean, General, that all of the other HVO artillery that you've just identified for us fell within the chain of command of the HVO Main Staff and was under direct control of the operative zones, the brigades, and the specific units that were in possession of those weapons, that -- whose job it was to use them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was your question, please? First of all, I didn't say that the 130-millimetre guns were not at their positions. I told you that there were two or three of them, so you should go back and read it again. That's what I said. Secondly, after the statement of yours, do put a question one at a time. Let's make things simple. You come up with six theses and then you ask me whether that was so or not. Which one do you have in mind? For the fifth time you're asking me the same thing. Commanding artillery falls under the responsibility of the person to whom that particular piece was assigned for a particular time and area to execute a task, an artillery piece of any sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But of course, General, based on -- from -- I'm just looking at what you've just said. You don't deny that if that individual soldier or group of soldiers uses artillery in an illegal way, and does so repeatedly, that they're the only people who are criminally responsible for using artillery in an illegal way; correct? Responsibility for unlawful use of artillery just doesn't end with the people who are firing the guns, does?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think Mr. Stringer should reformulate the question. It seems to me that the question only deals with the legal qualification of a certain event. He can ask about the facts which would lead him to a conclusion he wants to have, but he cannot ask about the legal qualification of it itself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know a single case of an American commander being held accountable for what happened in Iraq when -- where hundreds and thousands of civilians were killed due to reckless use of artillery. If you applied that logic to this case, I'll be immensely happy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The concept of the so-called collateral damage. But it seems to be -- this seems to employ a different logic. First of all, a group of people or a unit. A group of people is -- anywhere in the world can commit a crime, if that means that the entire social structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, General --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you did ask me about the legal formulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm not going to accept these sort of long rambling speeches. You're getting specific questions from me, and you may not like them, and it may be that there's someone here who could ask them better, but we're going to have to work together on this. We're going to have to get through this. You've testified a lot about your knowledge of the laws of war. You've told us that you know a lot and that you sought to educate others on the laws of war. We both know, General, don't we, that responsibility for the unlawful use of artillery does not necessarily end with the people who fire the weapons, that it can -- responsibility can, under certain circumstances, go to higher levels? Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We cannot. The responsibility of a senior level, if I have to answer that, exists only if an order arrived there that level or if by its silence it did not prevent such an incident from happening. In any other case, save for fascist societies, the person responsible is the individual who broke that particular rule. I don't know whether your opinion is different, but that was my interpretation of the laws of war. Responsibility lies only with the person who either issued an order or tacitly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, the Prosecutor is mentioning a legal issue that has to do with the responsibility, liability of the hierarchical superiors -- commander --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Of the commander, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a very complex question. I'm sure that the counsel has consulted with you on this, and he must have told you and he -- if he didn't he should have, but I'm sure he did. He should have told you that in the indictment you're also prosecuted under Article 7(3) of the Statute, and in Article 7(3) the -- there is a command responsibility under certain circumstances. That is the main principle here, and this is what the Prosecutor is actually talking about. Have you understood this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour Judge Antonetti. Even before the war I knew precisely what one can find in terms of responsibility in the laws of war. It is crystal clear where that responsibility is and where it ends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then you perfectly understand where the Prosecutor is going and what he wants to check with you. So please answer his questions. Mr. Stringer. This is where you were going; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, it's where I was going, Mr. President, but I think that I'm going to try to actually move away from the legal and back to some of the more factual before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I'm just looking at your testimony from a few minutes ago when you identified the various forms of HVO artillery that were targeting ABiH positions in East Mostar, and you're right, you said that there were --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And not only in East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, no. My question was about the artillery pieces that were targeting ABiH positions in East Mostar. That was my question, and I'm only interested in that right now. So let's go through the list you gave me, and if in fact it was something that was not deployed for ABiH positions in East Mostar you tell me. Okay?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of all weapons --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- was solely to repel the attacks of --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you that. Now, you said that there were 60-millimetre mortars. Those were deployed and were targeting ABiH positions in East Mostar after 24 July 1993. True or not true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not, Mr. Stringer. The 60-millimetre mortars are small pieces which are not directed --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't help you if you are ignorant of the use of a 60-millimetre mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me read --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I kindly ask the Judges to protect me from this type of ignorance. A 60-millimetre mortars is carried on one's back and moves back and forth. Could you please protect me from this type of ignorance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, earlier the Prosecutor asked you to list all artillery pieces and you did so. You agree with that. You told him there was a 60-millimetre, 82-millimetre, 120, and so forth and so on. That was the first step. Second step: Mr. Stringer is now asking you to tell us whether -- where these artillery pieces were deployed, positioned. And you said, "I can't help you if I don't have a map," et cetera, et cetera. The Prosecutor is now telling you, Very well, we don't have a map at hand, but as far as you recollect could you locate these artillery pieces. And then you told him, well, they were directed against the enemy, directed at the enemy. Fine, of course. And you gave no additional detail. But then the Prosecutor is pressing on and saying, I'll go through this case by case, you know, and he's going into details now. He's doing his job just like anyone else would have done, and he's now telling you about those 60-millimetre mortars, were they directed towards ABiH forces, and the answer must be yes or no. If you say no, you can explain why. If you tell us 60-millimetre mortars cannot be directed towards -- the city of East Mostar because the range is insufficient and so forth and so on, tell us. Say so. Then you're providing information to the Prosecutor and to the Trial Judges also. They're not technicians. Personally speaking, I can tell you I can't make a difference between a 62- and an 82-millimetre mortar. I have no idea, and I expect you to tell me, you to tell me a 60-millimetre mortar -- 60-millimetre mortar is such kind of artillery piece, has such and such range, can or cannot hit Mostar -- East Mostar, et cetera, et cetera. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, that's why I've been saying this. There is a question asked about the 60-millimetre, which is hand carried or slung over the shoulder. It can move along with the units five times a day. That's what it takes. It's not targeting anything specifically. There's an infantry attack that's launched, it takes a minute or two to mount it right there in front of you and then you fire it at whoever is attacking. How am I supposed to answer something like that, and the same thing applies to artillery weapons. If you have information indicating that the enemy is moving southwards, then you will be likely to check the multiple rocket launcher which is actually on wheels wherever it is that you are expecting an attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, why didn't you tell Mr. Stringer what you've just said? You should have told him that the 60-millimetre mortar is used by a soldier who is not turning it against any particular target. He only uses it if he is being attacked and if he receives an order. So this type of weapon does not have a target which has been set in advance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm trying but then I'm interrupted. I'm not here to harm anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, page 36, line 25, and page 37, the beginning, what the general just said to you is exactly what he started telling Mr. Stringer but was then interrupted and not allowed to finish. It's not that the general refuses to answer, he was interrupted in midstream.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, Mr. Praljak is telling us that this artillery piece does not have a predetermined target. It is used by a soldier according to the circumstances that occur. This is what the answer is. We shall have the break now, because we've overstepped the time and we shall resume after a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I hope -- [B/C/Son English channel].

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I think we're getting the B/C/S on the English channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It seems okay now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I want to come back to the various types of HVO artillery that we've been talking about, and in an effort to hopefully clarify and then be able to move on, I want to ask you -- ask it to you this way, and let's -- for our purposes I'm not interested anymore in where the artillery was located, okay, or whether it was moved. I want to ask you about the HVO artillery that was targeting ABiH positions in East Mostar from the 24th of July, 1993, until the 9th of November, 1993. So understanding that there are complications in discussing the locations of where those were, I'm not asking you to tell me where they were located, but I'm asking you about the types of artillery that were targeting ABiH positions in East Mostar during that period of time. So that's what my questions will be about. Now, earlier when I asked you about artillery that was targeting East Mostar ABiH, you mentioned 60-millimetre mortars; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, if I may just set the record straight in relation to one thing. The 60-millimetre, I classified it as such, not to simplify but let's not oversimplify, is not an artillery weapon. It's an infantry weapon. It's hand-carried or handheld or slung over one's back. It's not trained on anything. It's simply taken to wherever the unit is on its way to and used, and the same thing applies to other weapons. It gets moved around. It's not trained on something. A multiple-rocket launcher is stationary, covered with a piece of tarp when it's raining and it's not being used. Each weapon has a purpose, a use --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- a certain degree of mobility.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's forget about the 60-millimetre mortar then. Now, I'm looking at the transcript of the list that you provided us earlier, and you said that there was an 82-millimetre mortar. Can we agree that during the period of time that you were commanding the HVO Main Staff, 82-millimetre mortars were used by the HVO to target HVO positions in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 82-millimetre mortars were used to ward off attacks launched by the BH Army. That's the accurate answer. They weren't targeting East Mostar. They were targeting -- well, I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is BH Army attacks from East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why are we always talking about East Mostar? That's where the 4th Corps was, the 4th Corps of the BH Army. The units were mobile. They attacked in the south. They attacked in the city itself. They attacked -- how am I supposed to answer that one. It's just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, we are wasting our time, because you say yes to the question and then you provide us with additional details. You've just told us that the ABiH, the 4th Corps, was in East Mostar. You said that they were firing at you. And since they were firing at you, you retaliated. So you answered the Prosecutor's question by saying yes, 82-millimetre mortars did fire at the ABiH. That's your answer, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's true. Every time there was an attempt by the enemy to do anything in a military sense there was firing and targeting. I'm crystal clear about this. This was a war with two sides clashing, 82-millimetre mortars were used, 120-millimetre multiple rocket launchers. I'm not challenging that. I'm challenging the purpose of their use, the way they were used, the locations and so on and so forth. It's a lot more complicated than that moving this sort of equipment about. I'm just trying to put you in the picture of how this actually worked in a war setting, no more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The problem, General, is I'm not asking you about all of that additional information. I'm simply asking you what was used in respect of the ABiH positions in East Mostar. It's for others to decide whether the purposes and the methods and the means were appropriate or lawful, and I'm not asking you about any of that. I'm simply asking you what was the HVO artillery that was used against the ABiH that was in East Mostar, and I'm talking about the east side of Mostar town along the Neretva River, as well as, I guess for purposes of this discussion, the ABiH position that was along the narrow strip of the west side of the Neretva River. So now you've told us, in answer to Judge Antonetti's question, that the 82-millimetre mortars were used for that purpose. My next question is one that I think you've actually already answered. Maybe not. Were the 100 -- 120-millimetre mortars also used for the same purpose?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the attacks launched by the BH Army, everything was used to ward off these attacks, everything that I've listed, to the extent that was sufficient to actually ward off an attack: I have already confirmed that in purely military terms this was a bare minimum and this is also suggested by the overall number of shells as counted by SpaBat. There was nothing more than that. What was used was everything allowed under the rules of war to fend off attacks by the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In order to fend off attacks by the -- of the ABiH, as you put it, General, then you determined that it was appropriate and approved or authorised the use of HVO artillery to fire into East Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. You left it to your subordinates to determine what would be the use of HVO artillery in order to fend off ABiH attacks from East Mostar. Is that a better way of putting it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the law of war, they had every right and every responsibility to use any means available and allowed under those rules to fend off an enemy attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. And so I take that as an answer -- your answer is yes to my question, whether you left it to your subordinates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I'm not quoting any specific example. With the various documents we have at hand I could, but let me give you an isolated case. One day, for instance, in the month of August 1993, the ABiH fires from East Mostar and sends a projectile on the HVO. The unit which is standing close to where the projectile landed, if I understand what you are telling us, retaliates. The unit then uses one of its artillery pieces, whether it be 80 or 60-millimetre mortars, then fires back in the direction where it felt the projectile had come from. Without asking for any authorisation from the chain of command to do so, they shoot. Is that how things happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right with the following proviso: They had my oral orders to the effect that any response had to be kept to a minimum in every way, precisely because the BH Army often used forms of protection, and they fired from right in the middle of their own civilians, and that's why very often there had to be no response at all. For example, we're talking about Marsal Tito Street, or there had to be a minimal response if we were looking at a settled, built-up area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, you know better than anyone that there were army servicemen and civilians. I'm just quoting a theoretical example. Let's assume that an ABiH unit, a mobile unit, starts shooting knowing full well that there are civilians not far away, but they shoot and then they run away. The HVO retaliates. The HVO projectile will land on the civilians. Was this kind of example ever taken into account by the command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and I am putting it to you, Your Honours, that we targeted any soldiers walking around -- if we had targeted any soldiers walking around East Mostar, we would have been firing thousands and thousands of shells incessantly throughout. We were not firing, and it was strictly forbidden to fire at soldiers walking about East Mostar or, for example, if a single shell or two shells were fired from there. Even near the hospital there was some launchers positioned there, but there was no response from us, because it would have put the hospital in harm's way. All of their military -- had all of their military targets been destroyed, which would have resulted in the deaths of thousands and thousands of civilians, and we ourselves would have used up thousands and thousands of shells. There are lists of the overall number of shells fired, and there was a minimum use of artillery fire, and this precisely was the reason, to keep the civilian casualties down to nothing, if possible. There were zillions of BH Army soldiers in East Mostar, and if -- even if we had been applying the rules of war consistently throughout, I had every right in any of these situations to say, Fire away, it's a soldier over there, but I'm saying here under oath that is precisely what we were not doing. All we would resort to was the necessary response, and we tried to keep this outside any civilian areas to the extent that it was possible. If we had set about trying to destroy Donja Mahala, which contained their positions, nothing would have been left of it. Regardless of that, Donja Mahala was definitely a military target. That's the way the cookie crumbles a hundred times over.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, if you would move to the next document in the binder. It's P01424. General, we've been talking about different units or components of the HVO and recognise that this is a document that is from the period of time prior to your taking command of the HVO.
