This is from the 5th of February, 1993. It's an order of Bruno Stojic or for Bruno Stojic, and it's an order on the formation of units, and then it relates to municipalities under the jurisdiction of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And it's a rather simple question and not probably the most important one. There's a reference in paragraph -- well, there's 1.5, which is on the formation of units, and then item number point 1, I believe, or 1.1 says: "In all the municipalities under the jurisdiction of the HZ HB, Home Guard units in the organisational form posed by the Main Staff of the HVO, Croatian Defence Council." And then the next paragraph says that relates to in the first stage up to 28 February 1993, in all municipalities form Home Guard units as temporary bodies. And then I'm going to skip down where it says "Explanation of order," and then it says: "As a special part of the HZ HB armed forces, the Home Guard units are established to protect territories and facilities of special significance for the defence and provide support for the around forces." General, the question is simply whether the Home Guard units that are referred to here formed part of the organisation or structure of the HVO armed forces.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, General, the next document, unless there's any questions about the Home Guards based on that, is P00289. And we're going to change gears just a little bit here to talk about the HVO in perhaps more global terms. This is the first decree on the armed forces. It was later amended in October of 1992, General, but first question would be whether you were familiar with this document, say during the period of time October 1992 through June of 1992. Were you familiar with this document prior to the time you became commander of the HVO Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not familiar with this document as such, but I was aware of the fundamental guidelines regarding the armed forces. The basic structural framework that I thought I should be familiar with. I was familiar with that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Did you ever actually read this document or read the amended version of it that came out on the 17th of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, since you've indicated that you were familiar with the fundamental guidelines regarding the armed forces, I'll ask you a few questions about this, and if it's something you don't know about, just tell us. Just there in Article 2 it says that: "The defence system of the HZ HB shall be a unified form of organisation of the armed forces, administrative bodies, and legal entities with a view to ensuring the timely and organised prevention of attack or any other form of danger to the HZ HB." And then it says: "The armed forces shall be the main vehicle of armed resistance." So what this suggests, General, and you can tell me if you agree or not, is that the defence system, as a whole, has different components, different bodies, and those different bodies include the armed forces of the HVO that you were most closely linked to, but that it included other bodies, administrative bodies, and legal entities such as, perhaps, the Defence Department, and that those all formed a unity or a unified form of defence. Is that how you understood it to be based on what you saw?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is actually stated here quite accurately. The armed forces are made up of -- well, obviously some of it is the HVO and some other bodies are purely administrative but legal entities. Within the armed forces you get civilian police, military police, civil protection units and so on and so forth. A part of the armed forces is also constituted by the army itself to call it that, the HVO proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, we have to be careful about distinguishing between, as you've just put it, the army itself, the HVO, but then of course there's another HVO, if you will, which is the HVO HZ HB, which was, if I can put it this way, the government of the HZ HB, an executive or a civilian body; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I use the term, I limit myself to using it in relation to the military component of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But in fact, the HVO had an armed component or a military component as well as a civilian component; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And we see that reflected in Article 9. Can we agree on that? For example, we see here that the Croatian Defence Council shall do a number of things, and I wanted to try with you to see if we could distinguish between things that would fall within the competence of the military component and whether there are other tasks or responsibilities that fall within the responsibility of the civilian component. So where it says the Croatian Defence Council shall, number 1, adopt the defence plan of the HZ HB, General, would that be something that would fall within the responsibility of the HVO military, the HVO civilian, or both?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll repeat. The document is self-explanatory to varying degrees, depending on the person. I have no desire or intention to comment on it, the simple reasoning I wasn't one of the people who actually produced it. This document came into existence at a time when I held no official post at all. I would like to limit myself to talking about the tasks that actually concerned me, meaning the role and the location of the HVO Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I think that if you only commented on documents that you were actually involved in drafting, your direct testimony would have been a great deal shorter than it actually was. So we're going to stay with this, and I am going to insist on your comments here as someone who was highly active at the highest level of the military component of the HVO throughout 1992 and most of 1993. So recognising that you didn't write this, I'm asking you, based on what you saw, based on what you observed to be the practice and the things that -- the way things were operating, which body adopted the defence plan of the HZ HB? Was that the HVO military, the civilian component, or both?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I'm going to insist, Mr. President, that -- or that accused -- or if the accused who are making remarks, that the remarks be translated and put on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, the Prosecutor would like you to answer his questions based on this document. You have told us that this document is not something you authored. We know that. You don't have any direct knowledge of it, and you would like to stick to the purely military aspects of it. Military aspects are mentioned in different articles of this document. There are a number of articles which I believe you are able to comment about. If you don't know, just say so, but please contribute to these -- to these proceedings and help us establish the truth. This is what you have said when you started out. Insofar as you can, please answer these questions. Mr. Stringer, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, let me just put my question to you again so that it's fresh. Recognising that you didn't write this but based on what you saw, based on what you observed to be track the practice, the way things were operating, which body adopted the defence plan of the HZ HB? Was that the HVO military, the civilian component of the HVO, or both?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The defence plan was obviously adopted at a time when I wasn't there. I'm afraid I have to say that between the 24th and the 15th of October, and please don't for a moment forget this, throughout that time I would spend 20 hours a day waging war with no time to -- well, I can't possibly tell you something that I don't know. The HVO adopts a defence plan. Well, it must be written there. Surely it is. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honour, but I think we might be able to keep things less nervous if the Prosecutor asks the general if he knows about this plan, if he has seen it, knows whether it was adopted. We are talking about this plan assuming that the general knows about all of this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, was there a defence plan or wasn't there, because it is mentioned in the document, but was there one in fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, it's not for me to say, I don't think. I'm asking the general about a defence plan, Mr. President, and I'm asking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- about who was responsible for drafting a defence plan. Now, I can back up and ask the general does he know anything about a defence plan as referred to here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the defence plan, general?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So if there was one, you never saw it.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. What about number 2, stipulating measures for the improvement of the defence. Did you ever see whether any part of the HVO did that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then on determining the manner in which funds shall be raised and the level of funds needed to finance the tasks and needs of the defence. Now, surely, general, you must have knowledge of that side of things. Raising funds, allocating funds for the needs of the defence, would you agree with me that was largely within the sphere of responsibility of the HVO Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part I would agree, in part I wouldn't. I'm aware of the problem. It was an enormous problem within the HVO, the simple reason being this was causing additional chaos, utter chaos within the whole framework.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm not asking to tell about the financial difficulties. I'm asking you primarily or essentially which body or bodies were responsible for dealing with that, and I asked you specifically is this something that fell largely within the sphere of the ministry of defence, the Defence Department, or not? I don't need to know how difficult things were. I just need to know who's job it was to try to sort it out.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The job of finding money and, please, this is only in very conditional terms, that was down to the Finance Minister, and then probably he should have assigned this to the Defence Department, and the Defence Department was supposed to distribute this across the brigades in operation zones to meet people's needs, but there was no money to go around. We have an imaginary structure, again, in place here which has nothing to do with what goes on the ground. They go to Germany to collect money, and then one municipality has money, another municipality has no money, and now what are we trying to do? We're trying to get away from the truth and straight into speculation. So what do you expect me to do now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, we're looking at the document. I'm simply asking you under the terms of the document what were the various responsibilities for these -- these activities? Skip down to item number 6, the Croatian Defence Council shall decide on carrying out mobilisation. Now, was that something that was part of the military component, the civilian component of the HVO, or -- or both?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff did not deal with mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know which body did?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, not with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, item 7 is the HVO shall draw up plans to prepare the terrain for military operations, and then continuing to number 8, and undertake the other measures necessary --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, you should read out precisely. You read out Article -- item 7 wrongly. It draws up plans to determine the territory. I have no idea what it means, but it definitely doesn't mean what you said. You have to be precise too. I would like the interpreters to translate item 7 the way I read it out. It establishes plans to organise the territory. As I say, I have no clue what it means, but I know that it doesn't mean what Mr. Stringer said to the effect that it organised the territory in the military sense. I'm sorry, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may. Mr. Stringer is correct because he's reading the English translation, and the English translation is simply wrong. We have the words "for military operations," which seem to be added in the English translation and they're into the there in the original Croatian text.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number 7 says "determines plans to organise the territory." It has nothing to do with the army. What does that mean? In any case, this was simply copied from a different document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. So that -- item number 7, whatever it means, is something that does not fall within the sphere of the HVO military; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then item number 8 --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a second, sorry. [Interpretation] At this moment, I would kindly ask the Prosecutor, since this is his document, to use the appropriate procedure through the Registry to have the correct translation of this article so as to avoid any possible confusion in the future. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Of course we'll do that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, item number 8 says that the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please have it on the screen so that we can translate it; the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Can we put Article 9 of P00289 in e-court, if it's not already there. Article 9, item number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, General, can you read item number 7 again from the text that's in front of you. Just read it without comment.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Article 7, it determines the plans for the organisation of the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may add, I have no clue what it means, and I'm not sure the person writing this knew either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, the English translation seems to be a problem. "Draw up plans to prepare the terrain for military operations." Draw up the plan to prepare the terrain for something else. It has nothing to do, in fact, with the military operations. Actually, this translation is very strange. It's quite appalling, actually, you know, because this is really very different. Of course, you're not responsible for this translation. Fortunately, we have bilingual counsels, and sometimes they can find out these errors.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, what I want to do now is it turn to another part of this decree on armed forces. If you would turn to Article 21.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters ask for the Article 21 to be put on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. If we could blow-up Article 21 so that the interpreters can follow along as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, Article 21 of this Decree on Armed Forces says that: "The armed forces of the HZ HB shall constitute a form of organisation and preparation of citizens for armed struggle." Then it goes on to say that: "The armed forces of HZ HB shall protect its sovereignty, defend its territorial integrity." And concludes by saying that: "Every citizen of the HZ HB who, in an organised manner and in conformity with international law by bearing arms or in some other way, participates in resistance against the enemy shall be considered a member of the armed forces." General, what I want to do, bearing that text in mind, is to take you to the next exhibit in your binder, which is from the Constitution of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Article 162 of Exhibit 1D01236. Do you have Article 162 there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I believe, actually, we looked at this during an earlier -- or you commented on this during an earlier part of your testimony prior to this cross-examination, and recognising that the text is not identical as between Article 162 of the RBiH Constitution and Article 21 of the decree on armed forces, I do want to compare and contrast these two provisions for a few moments. If you look at the third sentence or the third clause found in Article 162 of the RBiH Constitution -- do you have that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What words are there at the beginning of the clause that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Article 162, the third clause says: "Every citizen who with arms or otherwise participates in resistance to the aggressor shall be considered a member of the armed forces of the republic."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And actually this article starts off by saying what the overall role or responsibility of the armed forces is, which is to protect independence, sovereignty, territorial integrity, unity, and the constitutional order of the republic. So you may or may not agree with me, General, but it would appear that although the text is not identical, these two provisions, one from the decree on armed forces and one from the RBiH Constitution, lay out in broad terms what is the role of the armed forces. Can we agree on that in broad, general terms? They seem to be roughly analogous provisions, I guess, is what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is similarity. However, I have to tell you something I have already stated before this Tribunal. You start with the presumption that this is the Constitution of the Republic of B and H, and I assert that it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's -- let's look at the next clause, the fourth clause in Article 162. It says: "With regard to the officer corps and appointments to the high command in leading positions in the army of republic, the principle of maximum proportional representation of the peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina and other peoples living in the country shall apply." Now, when I was looking at this provision earlier in your testimony, it occurred to me that that part, that provision or something like it is not found in the Decree on Armed Forces. There are not any provisions in the Decree on Armed Forces which mandate a principle of maximum proportional representations of the -- representation of the peoples. Would you agree with me that that is true, there is no mandate for maximum proportional representation of the peoples within the structure of the HVO armed forces?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such a provision does not exist, and there was no need for it, because the HZ HB was not a state and did not need to regulate such matters by way of provisions. It was implemented in practice, though, as the only armed force out of the forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was done for the most part throughout the armed forces as opposed to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I believe I have managed to show you through the documents that it did not comprise any Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So it was sort of a voluntary thing then in the HVO armed forces. There was no mandate or assurance, but it was something that could be done if the leadership of the HVO armed forces wanted to do that. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Article 21 there is no mention of ethnicities or peoples but of citizens. The HZ HB, much as its armed force, was based on its citizens, not peoples and ethnicities, and this is strictly prescribed in the provisions we saw. All citizens participating in it were equal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. And are you telling us that all of the Muslim people or all of the non-Croat people in the HZ HB were citizens of the HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. All citizens of HZ HB, as far as I know, were equal. As for the armed force, in terms of refugees, training, supply, to the extent I participated in Capljina and Stolac, as well as according to the witnesses we heard, no distinction was made between the citizens who chose to fight in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Right. But you didn't answer my question. My question was whether you're saying that all of the non-Croat people such as the Muslims who were living in the HZ HB, whether all those people were citizens of the HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I realise that Mr. Stringer can be at odds with General Praljak because of the interpretation. I will repeat again. Legally speaking there is a great difference between the word "gradanin" and the word "drzavljanin." The word "gradanin" that General Praljak keeps referring to, and that can be found in all HZ HB documents, means an inhabitant of a certain area. The word "drzavljanin," in our language, means that that person belongs or has the nationality of a certain state. I believe that the interpreters should use the word "gradanin" as "resident" in the English language rather than "citizen," because in that case Mr. Stringer is speaking at cross-purposes with General Praljak, wasting his words. I believe -- or, rather, I know that Mr. Buntic testified to this. I'm not testifying. I'm merely repeating a testimony we heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, this is -- counsel made the same intervention a few days ago or a couple of weeks ago. I can't remember exactly when it was, and I know that's the position of the Defence. It's my impression that the interpreters have a different position. They continue to give us the word "citizen" in English. And I don't want to put the interpreters in the middle of this, but maybe -- I don't know if it's possible to get some sort of an advisory opinion or some formal statement from the CLSS as to their position on the interpretation of these terms, but it may be that that's what's required, because otherwise we're going to continue to have this debate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's a complex problem, because it all depends on the meaning that you give to the word. When Mr. Praljak is using in his own language the word that is translated into English by "citizen," and when it seems that in reality he's talking about an inhabitant, then there might be a problem. In legal terms, a citizen is someone that has a nationality of a country, and a resident can live in another country -- can live in a certain country, can be a resident, an inhabitant of this country without having the nationality of this country. Let me give you an example. An American living today in Croatia would not be a Croatian citizen but would be an inhabitant or a resident of Croatia. So people use these words with different legal meanings, but when everything is translated we simplify everything and just say citizen. We don't know whether it's a full-fledged citizen or whether it is just an inhabitant and so forth. So, Mr. Stringer, to avoid the problem when you're really interested in all this, ask the witness what exactly he means by the word, because this is not the first time that counsels are raising to their feet. I believe that Mr. Kovacic already stood up, and it's always the same problem that crops up. All three Judges on the Trial Chamber come from countries where this idea of nationality is very well integrated. When you're a citizen of a state, it means that you have the nationality from the state. But when you're just a resident, a resident in the United States, it doesn't mean that you're a US citizen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, this wasn't really an issue that I was intending to go to -- into in depth with the general, and he was actually the one that was talking about equality for citizens, or at least that's how it was interpreted for me. So in order to avoid further spending time on this, I just propose to move on, and I would propose that perhaps we should follow up with the CLSS, which possibly would be a more productive way of getting to the bottom of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would still like to ask a question of Ms. Tomanovic who is here a sort of self-appointed but certainly knowledgeable language expert. Have I understood correctly that "gradanin" would be the resident, or have I mixed it up?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The word "gradanin" means inhabitant or resident. If you discuss -- if you recall the discussion with Mr. Buntic, it was about whether the HZ HB had the elements of a state or not. If the HZ HB in its documents speaks of "drzavljanin" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Nationals.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- then it has elements of a state, but it keeps referring to "gradanin," and that was what the discussion was all about with Mr. Buntic. Hence with all due respect towards the CLSS and its interpreters, I would suggest that this is not a matter of interpretation but of legal principle, and I believe the CLSS would not be fully competent to be the judge of it. I believe we have to go back to the testimony of Mr. Buntic, the attorney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm strongly reminded of the difference of "podrucje" and territory, where at one point the witness has told us that it was the same, actually. But coming back to this specific issue, that would mean that according to Article 21, every resident must be prepared for war, including the American who lives in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I must tell you I find that a very, very surprising proposal. I don't know of any country which regards residents, irrespective of nationality, as potential soldiers in the army of that country.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will respond given that I am a resident, and I have been a resident of that state for 50 years. The system of All People's Defence in our country was a unique one. There is no such like in the world. When we were 14, all of us were being prepared for any potential defence. This includes myself and all other colleagues sitting in this courtroom. I know that surprises you. That is why Dr. Prlic's Defence attempted to explain to you what a defence plan is. They provided you with the text of the Law on All People's Defence so that you would be able to see where things stood before the war. The HZ HB simply copied what had already existed in Bosnia-Herzegovina prior to the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Let's leave it at that for a moment. We cannot go into a long discussion, but there are several points that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prlic would like to take the floor. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] It is difficult for me to speak out among so many lawyers, but perhaps a suggestion having in mind the example of an American citizen living in any given territory. In our legal system two terms need to be differentiated. One is permanent residence, and temporary residence being the other. "Prebivalijte" is a place of permanent residence. "Boraviste" is something that can be given to an American. Our legal system was quite detailed in that fashion. It stipulated absolutely everything. For the most part it did not provide much room for interpretation. I don't know what translation of it is, but there is the word "prebivalijte" as opposed to "boraviste". However, a foreigner could not have been given the status of someone who has "prebivalijte," i.e., permanent residence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, if a foreigner who in 1993 would live in Bosnia-Herzegovina, according to Article 21, could he be integrated into the HVO for All People's Defence, which is what Ms. Tomanovic has explained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If that person had permanent residence, he or she could. Am I putting this correctly? And if that person was temporarily a resident there, if he there for, let's say, six months, spending a certain amount of time only in the country, then that person could not be integrated into the armed force. However, if that person was to be there for a longer period of time and hence was given permanent residence for whatever reason, say they got married but without receiving the nationality of that country, then that person could have been recruited into the HVO. That at least is my interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand you correctly -- let me sum things up. Let's talk about a Pole, for example, who would have been living for 15 years in Mostar. A Polish person with a Polish passport but he's been living in Mostar for 15 years so he has a resident card. Could he be integrated into the armed forces of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your Honour, many Muslims who had their permanent residence in, say, Rijeka or Split, working in the shipyards there, joined the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're telling us that in Croatia this case actually occurred, because Muslims working for example, in the shipyard in Split or in Rijeka -- [B/C/S on English channel]. Can you hear me now? Can you hear me now? Can you hear me now? You can hear me. Very well. So let's talk about a Libyan working in Split, a person from Libya who would have been living in Split for 15 years. According to you he could be incorporated into the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. In Sunja, for example, I had a person named Dr. Eid, who was a physician with the Croatian army, and he served in the local unit, and he was from Lebanon or some place like that. He obtained his degree in Croatia, and he just stayed on. He had a Lebanese nationality, obviously, but he was also part of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I think it's a bit clearer now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, we had just been looking, as you know well, at Article 21, and I had asked to you about the fact that this principle of maximum proportional representation was not included within the decree on armed forces, and I believe you -- you said that that's because it wasn't necessary to have such a provision; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was included in the provision concerning citizens. We did not want to write anything about proportional representation which no one would adhere to, as opposed to this definition as citizens, as inhabitants of a certain area or whatever else you like to call it. So they were represented in proportion to the number of citizens belonging to various ethnicities who are in the area. I will continue to challenge this version of the BH Constitution, though. There is no law under which this Constitution could be adopted, not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If you please turn to Article 28 of the Decree on Armed Forces. This says that the Croatian language and the Latin script shall be used in the armed forces of the HZ HB. Now, the fact is that you said wasn't -- the principle of maximum proportional representation wasn't included in here. The fact is that the addition or the requirement of the use of the Croatian language was indeed intended as something that would signal that in fact the armed forces of the HVO was to be largely or primarily or in its essence a Croatian armed forces.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not necessarily what follows. In Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, Serbo-Croatian or Croato-Serbian, if you like, was the official language. Given the power scale and method of the aggression carried out by the JNA or the army of RS, it would have been quite impossible for anyone at the time to accept to use the language of an aggressor. Unfortunately, Muslims and Bosniaks did not at the time have a name for their own language. It came later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, General --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But at the time anything else was entirely ruled out other than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The fact is that I know that -- I don't want to -- it can be a delicate subject and I don't want to offend anybody, but the fact is that during this period of time, in the summer and the fall of 1992, throughout 1993, whether you were a Croat or a Muslim or a Serb, you could be speak and you could be understood easily by someone who was a member of a different ethnic group, and the fact was there's no need at all to specify or to mandate any particular language in order to ensure that members of the armed forces could communicate; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The use of language in the armed forces must be defined. Your interpretation of language in terms of who understands who else and what follows from that displays a method and a level that unfortunately prevents me from contributing to this in any way because of the level of questions asked. Each of the various ethnic groups in Yugoslavia had every right to call their language whatever they liked.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And this particular provision, was it taken with any sort of consultation or input from people who didn't consider themselves to be Croatian? Is there any accommodation made for them, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. But I do know that at the time no conclusion was adopted about what language the Bosniaks would be using. In Tuzla, if I remember correctly, Mr. Prlic's witness -- one of Mr. Prlic's witnesses -- fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next exhibit is P004 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, we have just seen a series of articles, Article 21 and 28. Remember, Mr. Buntic had also talked about these. As far as I remember, all these decrees had been prepared by the competent departments and had then been adopted at two meetings since it was on the agenda, and without any more ado all these articles had been adopted. Based on that, one can assess this in two ways: The Prosecutor's position is that all these articles reflect the joint criminal enterprise; namely, to establish a Croatian community that is autonomous, that has its own territory, and so on. That is why Article 28 stipulates that the Latin script and the Croatian language should be used. That would be the first theory. The second would be more of a constitutional nature. Do all these articles comply with the Constitution? The Prosecutor prepared Article 21 with Article 160, I believe, of the Constitution, and as far as the language issue is concerned, he did not mention Article 4 of the Constitution which entitles anyone to use Serbo-Croatian, Croatian-Serb, the Cyrillic transcript, the Latin transcript, and/or both since all these should be equal, and the following question came to my mind: The person who drafted this, I don't know whether the person who drafted this text was perhaps an intern, a legal expert, I don't know, and he is being asked to -- he or she, to draft Article 21. The person in question takes the text of the Constitution and sees that the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina are in charge of the protection of the integrity and sovereignty of the territory, and he just uses the same terms and places them in Article 21, and in the Constitution there are also provisions relating to the use of -- to -- of the Serbian, Croatian, and Bosnian language. This is not mentioned, however. Do you think this is plausible or was everything thought through? There is in Article 21 a very heavy charge here. "The armed forces of the HZ HB must protect the sovereignty and defend the integrity of the territory," which means that Herceg-Bosna in this case has its sovereignty and territory. So you understand what I'm saying. These are the exact words of the Constitution. So I wonder whether the people that drafted this article understood everything or whether this meets the requirement of a very precise plan which is the case put forward by the Prosecutor. What do you have to say to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, when one looks at this individually and when there is mention of the word "sovereignty," obviously, this might indicate that this entity has the ambition of becoming a state, but, Your Honours, we cannot dwell on a single word in this trial. At the same time, the HZ HB, within the framework of Bosnia and Herzegovina, remains right there until a final determination is made. On the other hand, territorial integrity is a phrase that was probably adopted from somewhere else. It was copied. There was no territorial integrity to speak of in the case of the HZ HB. These were 30 minor entities within Bosnia-Herzegovina. If one defends the sovereignty of, for example, a part of the Bosnia and Herzegovina, recognising itself to be in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you thereby defend Bosnia and Herzegovina, a country which had broken up. Secondly, even if it were possible to assume that a thing like this might contain some sort of criminal enterprise, how is it possible to create Republika Srpska in Dayton as a part of that state? This is the very implementation of a criminal enterprise or criminal plan. All people who did that should be brought to face this court and we should abolish Republika Srpska because it ended up implementing a criminal enterprise that is not even mentioned here. My -- my brain is facing a conundrum. I have no problem admitting that. There are whole parts and portions of this trial and phrasings such as these that I fail to understand. Citizens. We got citizens organised to defend our very livelihood, our lives. It was within the framework of Bosnia-Herzegovina that we actually managed to preserve that country. And secondly, Your Honours, everyone seems to be referring to the 1991 census which the assembly never legally ratified because it didn't have the last item there and cannot be used. Likewise, this is not the BH Constitution. We keep saying that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, I stop you there, because my question was a very precise one and now you are talking about the 1991 census, and you've explained to us already what all of this has to do with -- you have answered my question. I'm satisfied with that, and my colleague would like to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I cede precedence to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, if I may, and I do apologise for interrupting and springing to my feet before you ask your question, but there is one thing that I find to be of considerable significance, something I had expected Mr. Praljak to say and he didn't, and this is because of Judge Antonetti's question. When you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm going to object to this, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption, but I don't think it's appropriate for counsel to jump up and to -- to supplement or to add to something that Praljak didn't say that she was expecting him to say. I don't think that's appropriate. It's -- we've exhausted this issue, and now counsel are beginning to testify and we object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are quite right. You are right. One moment, Ms. Nozica. Mr. Stringer is right. You cannot interrupt now to add to what Mr. Praljak should have said. However, if there is a mistake or something important in that line, that you can mention. I don't know what you wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour, there is, an enormous error, the error being one needs to look at the dates. Throughout this cross-examination by my learned friend, I was bearing this in mind. I thought it might be observed at some point. One must look at the date of the decree on the armed forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and also the date the Constitution was adopted. Mr. President, you asked why the Decree on the Armed Forces did not include any provisions of the Constitution. That would have been impossible. However, because the decree on the armed forces, which is P289, was not adopted before the 3rd of July. The next Decree of the Armed Forces of the HZ HB was adopted in October 1992; whereas, the Constitution being shown to us by my learned friend, Mr. Stringer, was adopted as clearly seen on page 1 on the 24th of February, 1993. Therefore, this cannot be prepared and cannot be cross-examined on in terms of whether these provisions were supposed to constitute a substantial element of the BH Constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. We could have actually used another document which would have been the Yugoslav Constitution, because a lot of the parts of the Bosnian Constitution stemmed from the Yugoslav Constitution. There was a fair chance that the articles we've seen were most certainly part of the Yugoslav Constitution. We haven't actually seen that, but my colleague would like to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, and it relates to Article 28, the article on the language in the army, and you have said that it was necessary to state this. My question is: Are you aware of any other than the Croat language and any other script than the Latin script being used in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, I'm not aware. I don't know if the Serbs, as these days in Croatia, were entitled to use their own Cyrillic script or not. This is only about the armed forces. In the former Yugoslavia there was a single language to be used by all the peoples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It might be the right time to have a break now. In ten minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Ten minutes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I'm going to put this to you, and I'm putting it to you and it's also in a sense a response to some of the comments made by counsel for Mr. Stojic now, who pointed out that the decree on armed forces, both versions, came into existence prior to the time of this -- of the RBiH Constitution. I'm putting to you, General, that in fact is doesn't matter what these two documents -- the difference in these two documents, the armed force -- Decree on Armed Forces on the one hand and the RBiH Constitution on the other, the difference in the texts show us what were the differences in the approach that were in the heads of the people that wrote these documents. I'm going to put it to you that on the HVO side we do not have any principle of maximum proportional representation because that's not something that the HVO leadership were interested in having in its Croat armed forces. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it's not true. In each and every municipality, everywhere based on what I've heard here and what I knew back then, everything was in keeping with the election results and the representation of Croats, Muslims, and Serbs was equal; all those who went to the elections. And anyone could join the HVO -- and I could give you examples, if you like, to illustrate this. From Mostar's commander, who was a Muslim, Croats --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm going to put the Prosecution case to you and I expect that you'll disagree with me. Secondly, I want to put it to you that in fact the provision in the Decree on Armed Forces imposing the Croatian language and the Latin script is there, and that it differs so significantly from the analogous text in the Constitution of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which the President pointed out, those very huge differences in approach on language are also a result on the HVO side of a desire or an intention to have an exclusively Croat or an essentially Croat armed forces in the HZ HB; isn't that also true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most certainly not. In addition to that, at the time there is no such things as Bosnia and Herzegovina. There is nothing actually called Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time. A large part of one of the peoples involved attacked the two other peoples --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. General --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just in order to mobilise -- all right. I entirely disagree with you, and most of all what you're putting to me and what you're trying to prove is not accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next exhibit is P00441. And, General, this is an HVO training plan and programme for conscripts that was approved by your predecessor, Brigadier Milivoj Petkovic. It's dated the 1st of September, 1992, so this came out about seven weeks or so before you went to Prozor, and I want to talk about some parts of this as we further discuss the essence or the vision of the HVO armed forces that was being formed as of this period of time. Have you ever seen this training programme before, General?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I stole a cursory glance. My assistants were busy working on a programme that I signed much like this one, perhaps a little more specific. I seem to remember that at the time I cast a quick glance over it. The previous one, too, of course. They had it right there on their table. I may have, but I can't be entirely certain. I think for the best -- best part at one point in time I did leaf through it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You have -- have actually -- you've referred to your own training programme that you and your people put together, and we're going to get to that. That's the next document that's in your binder. So we'll talk about General Petkovic's programme first and then we'll talk about yours. General, the part in this exhibit, P0441, that I'm interested in is the section on the upbringing in the spirit of patriotism which there's a reference to it here in the first table that appears in the document. It's on page 5 of the English translation. It's under the section on the plan. And then moving to page 7 of the English, General, do you see a section in this document concerning the upbringing in the spirit of patriotism?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't locate that. What page is that in the Croatian document?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'll see if I can direct you to that. Do you see the table here where we have "Training subjects," and then we have different --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you look at the page number up there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm looking at the table. Do you have a table in yours? THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] R103927.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I'll try and find that. 3927. I don't have any tables there. Oh, right, right, right. Yes, yes, yes. I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then you'll see another table that relates to the subject of -- under -- under paragraph 1.3. Do you see paragraph 1.3?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What page is that? Can I have the ERN number --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Number 4, table 1.3 is on page 4 of the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And, General, actually, if you'll continue on. The page that I want to take you to is stamped with the RR103927?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 6 in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, are you with me on page 6 of your version, "Upbringing in the Spirit of Patriotism"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, it says here that the goal of the subject is to lift and strengthen feelings for the homeland as well as morale and psychological characteristics of the training programme to inform the training participants about the history and the present times of the Republic of Croatia and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Now --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not quite how it reads. Since we're quoting, can we please try to be accurate. Subject number 1, subject number 2, subject number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I think you're jumping ahead of me, General, so if you'll just bear with me. I'm looking at a topic called "Upbringing in the Spirit of Patriotism." Underneath that I'm looking at words that say goal and task of the subject. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then the part I just read.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, all right. I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, what this means, General, is that the reference there to the homeland is in fact a reference at the very least to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says. To be familiarised with the history of the Republic of Croatia and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, but Herceg-Bosna extended all over Bosnia and Herzegovina, so there's no reason to -- but, then again, I have to say that in addition to the political structure and the defensive character, Herceg-Bosna was the same as Bosnia and Herzegovina. We don't know whether this is in reference to -- Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know these texts which -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm going to have to --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: -- questions --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm sure we'll ask Mr. Petkovic about this when he testifies, but I'm asking you about it now as someone who was highly active within the HVO and -- during the period of time shortly after this was issued. The fact is, General, isn't it that the training programme of the HVO, as from September of 1992, really did not have any goal, the building of any sort of spirit of patriotism or feelings for the true homeland of the people who were living in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was in fact the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Isn't that true? This is only about the homeland being a narrow part of that country called Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what follows from this. Herceg-Bosna might here be synonymous with Bosnia-Herzegovina. Then again, I challenge your right to tell me what my homeland is. Country and homeland is not the same thing. Bosnia and Herzegovina was drawn up in Berlin.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obeying the wishes of Bismarck and all the rest of them. You can't go telling me what my homeland means, whereas you can't force me -- force upon me a definition of what my state or country will be. These are two different things. You drew up countries as you saw fit, but there's nothing you can do about homelands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, I recall what the President has warned you this morning. Listen carefully to the questions. Mr. Stringer has not spoken of your personal homeland at all, not at all. So you don't have to complain that someone else is trying to attribute or not attribute any homeland to Mr. Slobodan Praljak. It was another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, maybe it's a good time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, when we had the break we were looking at the training programme for the HVO that was approved by General Petkovic on 1st of September, 1992. And just to continue with this programme on upbringing in the spirit of patriotism, if you move down from the text we were reading before, you get to the "Programme subjects." And there is number 1 is an introduction, and then number 2 is the various topics involved, which include the Republic of Croatia and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in the war for freedom. Second topic is history of Croats in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. We see the other topics, 3 and 4, on the armed forces, training on the defence -- decree on defence of the HZ HB under topic 4. Topic 5 is HZ HB foes, which includes facts about anti-Croatian activities, Serbian political parties, et cetera. Now, General, do you know, and maybe you don't, was this training applicable even to Muslims and non-Croats who were members of the HVO armed forces at this time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As long as that was possible, it applied to all HVO units from Bihac, Tuzla, or anywhere else in Bosnia-Herzegovina. There would be a total of five hours, which amounted to 2 per cent of the overall training time. An insignificant amount of time to cover these five topics. To be perfectly honest, I subscribe to all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Perhaps it's not insignificant if you're a Muslim member of the HVO who's been putting his life on the line up to this point in time fighting against the Serbs, and then he shows up at this programme and all he's going to hear about is the history of Croats and the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. It elevates one group above the others, doesn't it, within the HVO arms forces among the conscripts, the foot soldiers themselves.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think not. Why? The history of Herceg-Bosna is a history shared by Croats and Muslims alike. As for the tasks of the armed forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, they were meant to protect the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. It had to do with the Muslims, the Croats, and the Serbs as long as they wanted to be a part of this enterprise. I do remember quoting some literature in the document that I produced. The attempt here was to spend as least time as possible to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. You just made reference to your own training programme. You've indicated that you subscribed to the programme that we just looked at from General Petkovic. So let's go ahead and look at your programme, which is P04142.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I subscribed to this programme. There is talk there of moral backbone, and there are further topics that are elaborated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, General, 4142, which for the record is also Exhibit 3D01229, and, General, you testified about this document already on the 2nd of June, according to my notes. Do you remember seeing this and talking about it during an earlier part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember a little, yes. I'll take your word for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I'm looking at the third page of the English, just at the very beginning of the document, which is the -- I guess the order, if you will, in which you direct that this programme is to come into effect on the 12th of August, 1993. This is at the very beginning of the document. So for purposes of the time-frame, General, can we agree that you had this training programme prepared, you approved it, and you ordered that it come into effect within a fairly short period of time after you took over the command of the HVO Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can agree on that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I'm going to move to page 10 of the English language version which in your version, General, is the page that has the ERN stamp which ends with 0837. If you could look at the stamped number 0837. Have you found that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed I have, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And this is under V, the training programme, and it's got a list of eight topics or subject areas in which the trainees are to receive training, and here we see -- I'm going to focus on item number 2, which is the "Homeland education" part for the time being, but perhaps at this point, General, would it be correct to say that the training that these conscripts are to receive, your intention is that they receive basic military training on how to hold and fire a weapon, how to perhaps move throughout the terrain, how to work in groups, various basic aspects of -- of military training that conscripts or people who are just joining the military for the first time would received? Is that sort of your target group for this programme?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't just for those who joined the programme, but also those who had not previously been properly -- properly trained or undergone appropriate training. Even in the middle of a war, the circumstances being what they were, we tried to raise both the moral and the cognitive levels of the soldiers to make sure that they were familiar with all the elements that a confrontation like this normally entailed, leaving them fully prepared. I'm not going to read on, but it was about the stress relief. It was about fear. It was about respect. It was about adherence to regulations of the rules of war, the rules of engagement, everything that was required, and we tried to achieve this as swiftly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, among the course titles indicated under this training programme, what we do not find and what we do not find throughout this entire document is a reference to training on the rules, the laws of war that would apply to soldiers and the way in which they are to treat civilians, the way in which they're to conduct themselves lawfully in carrying out their activities as soldiers. Isn't it true you failed to include international humanitarian law, the law of war, in your training programme?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is entirely untrue. If you like, at the very outset make sure the soldiers are able to behave as regular proper soldiers. That was part of the moral education section. And then there were several seminars that were organised, and every time there was talk of the Law of War.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So are you telling us, General, that those seminars and that training would take place separately from this training programme that we're looking at now?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both within the framework of the programme, and then there were separate special seminars with the Red Cross people. Tens of thousands of booklets and brochures were distributed on these occasions, and that was going on right from the very outset. I have said a number of times already I worked on that even while I was still with the Croatian army, and I have already provided all the evidence to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, then to focus in on the programme on homeland education, since this is your document and since you reacted to my last question about the homeland part of General Petkovic's programme, let me ask you, when you wrote or approved this programme on homeland education, what homeland were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anything that had to do with an accurate rendition of the history and area covered by the former Yugoslavia and the Croats in it, as well as the Serbs and the Muslims. Forty years of history twisted and inaccurately interpreted. We only have very few hours to work with, very little time, but we had to do something to have all of this established on a sounder foundation than used to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, turning to page 14 of the English, this is page 0839 of your version, General. This gives us more information about the homeland education programme, and the objective and task as set out in this is to "participate in the formation of such intellectual, moral, professional, and personality features of the Croatian soldier (the HVO soldier) that promote patriotism and motivation required for successful and efficient implementation of task." It goes on to say: "Provide basic knowledge of Croatian history, civilisation, culture, and state-building tradition ..." and then "... the centuries-old arduous struggling of Croatian people and the moral values of Croatian lands." Now, General, I recognise that this document that you're issuing around the 12th of August, 1993, is one that comes after the events of 30 June 1993, and so that I think we could agree that by this point in time the gloves were off as we say, back where I come from, in terms of outright and full conflict between the ABiH and the HVO; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part. There was not a full conflict between the ABiH and the HVO, and it was not a conflict. It was an attack by the BH Army on certain components of the HVO, and, yes, the gloves were off in that respect, especially as concerned certain units of the BH Army, certain commanders, and certain policies that were perceived. Not overall, though, as we have witnessed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I accept that correction on your part. What we do know is that by this point in time all Muslim members, men who had been members of the HVO in the areas of the North-west and South-east Herzegovina operative zones had been disarmed. They'd been removed from the November and had been put into detention facilities. Can we agree that that was the context, that's what's happening at or about the time that this training programme came out?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't go into anything that occurred before my time. Most Muslims in the HVO did what they did on the 30th of June, 1993, but by no means all of them. A number still remained in the area, a number of Muslims in the ranks of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Particularly in the area of Posavina and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I -- in my last question I limited it deliberately to the area falling within the North-west Herzegovina and South-east Herzegovina operative zones, and so that's what I want to limit our discussion to at this point. I certainly recognise that the situation in the Posavina was different. But within those areas of the south-east and north-west operative zones, we had a virtual complete disarming and detention of Muslim males who had been members of the HVO; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm that what you said about complete disarming and detention simply because I did not have any accurate information regarding that after I came. Disarming, yes, but detention, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. We'll be talking about that later. The point for purposes of the discussion now is that really by the 12th of August, 1993, the gloves are off as -- as we've said, at least within this area of North-west and South-east Herzegovina operative zones, so that really the fact is that by this point the HVO armed forces are an exclusively, or virtually exclusively, Croatian armed force and so that the training and the homeland formation that's going to be given relates exclusively to Croatian people; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term that you employed, the gloves are off, is a diplomatic term and has no meaning whatsoever in the military context. What I know is this: At the time there was an aggressor and someone else who was defending. Be it moral values, be it general behaviour, be it criminal offences, be it history, nothing whatsoever was changed in the education programme in relation to what it would normally have been. There was no training indicating any changes like that. Quite simply one had to make sure history was interpreted faithfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There had been a twisted interpretation of history for the previous 40 years and that misinterpretation was used for ideological purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, wouldn't you agree with me, General, that the entire orientation of this training, whether it's yours or whether it's General Petkovic's, is an orientation toward exclusively Croatian people and Croatian soldiers as members of the HVO based on what we're seeing in these documents?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it is that you're seeing in these documents. If there's something you're seeing as you say, please point it out to me. Obviously one needed --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the general please be asked to repeat this. We didn't understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. The interpreters didn't quite catch what it was you were just saying. I was going to cut you off anyway, to be perfectly honest with you. You said -- you said -- I put it to you that this was an exclusively Croatian orientation in these documents. You wanted me -- you suggested that I wasn't pointing you to specific parts of these documents that I had in mind, but let me point you very -- right back to these two provisions that we've just looked at, that we've just read out, that this training on homeland education relates to training on participation in the formation of the various features of the Croatian soldier, the HVO soldier, or here the Croatian soldier is equated with HVO, and then the next passage that involves providing basic knowledge of Croatian history, civilisation, culture, centuries-old arduous struggle of Croatian people, the moral values of Croatian lands. The fact is that these passages make it clear that the HVO is nothing but an exclusively Croatian militia whose orientation is towards the Croatian people alone; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, what this is about is showing the truth. Homeland education is about showing the truth, and these topics are designed in such a way as to expose the truth that had led to the war. It is not only an attempt to defend the Croats. It is also an attempt to defend the 10.000 Muslims in West Mostar, the 3.000 Serbs in West Mostar. The talk here is about honour, loyalty, order, structure, morale, freedom, peace, democracy, future. These are topics that must be addressed by any civilised human being. These are truthful topics. This is not just some sort of Croatian-only policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in Bosnia-Herzegovina of all places, do you think it's possible to give an accurate treatment to all of those issues when you're talking only about one group of people, Croatian people and their history? The fact is it's impossible to do that unless you're wishing to provide an exclusive orientation that instills in these conscripts only one, only one objective which is to defend Croatian people and Croatian territory. That is what this is about, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Defending Croats across Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croats and all the other men defending -- being defended by those units throughout the area including Zenica, Tuzla, Sarajevo, and Bihac. When you talk about the history of the Croats, sir, it is not possible to say nothing about all the others, about Garasanin, about Karadzic, Moljevic, the Chetnik Movement and so on and so forth. I'm all too familiar with this topic, and what you see listed here is everything that is helpful terms of allowing these people to know the truth, the truth that was being built on as a political topic and which led to the war. It was for these people to know what they would be killed for. And also, among other things, Mr. Stringer, to defend all the Croats wherever they were. That much is true, but not just the Croats, not the Croats alone. It was about getting themselves killed. For the refugees also. For the 500.000 Muslim refugees not to be trampled underfoot the way they were in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's what we were getting ourselves killed for and that's what this homeland education was for. The wounded, the weaponry. One needed to lay a proper foundation for all of this because only that made sure there was a proper approach to all these things, and I still stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And yet these conscripts, the message is, you just said it, is that they've got to stop and prevent themselves from being trampled underfoot the way they were in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The message is that these conscripts aren't fighting for a Bosnia-Herzegovina are they. They're fighting for that autonomous Croatian area that we've been talking about all week long where the Croat people were going to have the majority ethnic composition so that they could govern this autonomous area and that's what these conscripts are being taught to fight about, to fight for. Isn't that true? This has nothing to do with Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is the country in which you find yourselves?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not true. This was taught both in Sarajevo and in Tuzla, and in Posavina, and in Bihac, and in [indiscernible]. What were they defending there? Why all the casualties in these areas that could never possibly have become what you referred to as the Banovina or indeed territory belonging to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, let's move to the bottom of this section, then, and look at the last phrase that appears in this section. We're going to skip down two bullet points. This is still under number 1, Objective and Tasks of Homeland Education. Now, the last point in that section says: "On the basis of information acquired, guide and motivate soldiers to actively participate in the defence and development of HZ HB." Now, General, what you're telling us now is not true. There's nothing in here about Bosnia-Herzegovina. There's nothing in here about Tuzla or the Posavina or anywhere else. This is your HVO, and the fact is, General, that your HVO is only about Croat people defending this Herceg-Bosna that's going to be your autonomous Croatian area. Isn't that the way it really was?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The HZ HB all -- was made up of all the municipalities that joined the organisation, and there's a list of that. When I led the attack on the Neretva's left bank, where there were relatively few Croats, I wasn't just defending the Croats there. We used 90 per cent of the HVO's entire manpower to fight for Bosnia and Herzegovina and all the citizens that were being subjected to this aggression. I put my life on the line each and every day there for that country, for each and every citizen, of course including my own people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: But not during the time that you were commander of the HVO Main Staff. The fact is, General, that during late 1992 and throughout 1993, you had very little, if anything, to do with any of the conflicts that were taking place outside the territory of the HZ HB. You were not in Tuzla. You were not in Posavina. You were moving back and forth from Herzegovina to Zagreb. You were coming back down to Prozor, Tomislavgrad, Gornji Vakuf, and throughout that period of time you only addressed yourself and your activities to this area of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and not any other Croatian community anywhere else; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I fought hard in Posavina in the summer of 1992 as well. I was in Vares as well. I was in Kiseljak. I offered to help lift the siege of Sarajevo to Alija Izetbegovic. Wherever I went --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Praljak. I could repeat myself. Listen carefully to the question before you start answering. The question explicitly was limited to the time when you were at the head of the HVO, and now you have spoken of previous times. That was not included in the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise. I thought it was a more general question. That's the way it struck me, relating to the entire period, but we should check the transcript. I thought it was about me only moving about those areas, including earlier on in the way specified by Mr. Stringer. I may be wrong though, but during the time that I was commander of the Main Staff, I never went beyond the borders that were sort of marked and established by the aggression of the BH Army. There was no way I could cross those borders.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, General --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even in those conditions we allowed the BH Army weapons to go through immediately and permanently and unconditionally just in order not to see them lose the war to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me put it to you this way, General: Certainly from October of 1992, you were only in place where is there was conflict between the HVO and the ABiH, Prozor, Gornji Vakuf, Mostar, North-west Herzegovina operative zone, South-east Herzegovina operative zone. And the fact is you were never were areas where the HVO, the Muslims and the Croats were fighting well alongside each other against the Serbs; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is also not true. There were no clashes in Mostar at the time. Among other things, I was involved in the joint defence of the Croats and Muslims in Travnik after the fall of Jajce. You've heard evidence to that effect. I helped allay the tensions to do with the clashes that had erupted, and I was very successful in bringing about a lull in the fighting. There are plenty of documents showing that. Up until the very last minute I worked on the cooperation between the HVO and the Supreme Command of the BH Army. I made an enormous effort to keep clashes from erupting to see how the state itself would be structured to avoid clashes and so on and so forth. Every single thing that you have just put to me is untrue.
